title: Global Market Outlook: US Jobs Report, Treasury Yields, Oil Prices and Fed Policy in Focus
intro:
Wall Street Awaits US Jobs Report as Treasury Yields, Oil Prices and Middle East Tensions Keep Markets on Edge

Global markets remain cautious as investors focus on the US labor market and its potential implications for the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy. US stock futures were little changed on Friday ahead of the September employment report, while elevated long-term Treasury yields and escalating tensions between the United States and Iran continued to shape market sentiment.
The market environment remains particularly challenging. On one hand, the US economy continues to show signs of resilience. On the other, rising energy prices and higher long-term borrowing costs risk keeping inflationary pressures elevated, potentially complicating the Fed’s policy outlook.
Meanwhile, crude oil remains above $90 a barrel, the US dollar is extending its recent gains, and gold continues to face pressure from the combination of elevated Treasury yields, dollar strength and geopolitical uncertainty.

WALL STREET: MODEST REBOUND AHEAD OF NONFARM PAYROLLS
Wall Street’s major indices closed slightly higher on Thursday, recovering part of their early losses as selling pressure across global bond markets eased.
The S&P 500 gained 0.19% to close at 7,666.45, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average and Nasdaq Composite both advanced 0.04%, ending the session at 50,926.56 and 26,871.60, respectively.
Investors are now turning their attention to the September US employment report, which could provide important clues about the health of the economy and the Federal Reserve’s next policy moves.
Economists expect approximately 90,000 new jobs, with the unemployment rate forecast to remain unchanged at 4.1%. However, following the recent surge in Treasury yields and renewed concerns about inflation, markets may require particularly strong employment data before significantly increasing expectations for another Fed rate hike this month.
Traders currently assign approximately a 75% probability to interest rates remaining unchanged.

TREASURY YIELDS: 10-YEAR YIELD HITS HIGHEST LEVEL SINCE 2002
The bond market remains one of the main sources of pressure across financial markets.
The US 10-year Treasury yield briefly climbed to 5.34%, reaching its highest level in approximately 24 years, before retreating partially toward the end of Thursday’s session.
The move reflects a combination of factors, including expectations surrounding Federal Reserve policy, persistent inflation concerns, rising energy prices and growing attention to the sustainability of government debt.
Higher yields are also tightening global financial conditions, increasing borrowing costs and making long-duration bonds less attractive relative to other investment opportunities.
Rate-sensitive sectors, particularly real estate and banking, remain exposed, while rising Treasury yields continue to pose a challenge for equity valuations, especially across the technology sector.

US SECTORS: ENERGY LEADS GAINS AS MATERIALS AND RATE-SENSITIVE STOCKS LAG
At the sector level, Energy was the strongest performer during Thursday’s session, gaining 1.93% within the S&P 500, supported by rising crude prices and escalating geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.
In contrast, Materials recorded a particularly sharp decline, while real estate and banking stocks underperformed as higher borrowing costs weighed on sentiment.
Chip-design companies and selected semiconductor stocks showed relative strength, highlighting the increasingly differentiated performance within the technology sector.

STOCK MOVERS: ACCENTURE AND SYNOPSYS RALLY, NIKE COMES UNDER PRESSURE
Among the biggest individual stock movers, Accenture surged 15.8% after reporting quarterly revenue of $18.7 billion, beating expectations of $18.0 billion.
The company also reported new bookings worth $22.2 billion and forecast fiscal 2027 revenue growth of between 3% and 6%.
Synopsys also posted strong gains, climbing 12.8% after presenting a new multi-year growth framework. The company outlined ambitious fiscal 2027 targets, alongside partnerships with Amazon and OpenAI and an AWS licensing agreement worth more than $1 billion.
Nike moved in the opposite direction, falling nearly 5% after reporting quarterly revenue of $11.2 billion, below the $11.4 billion consensus estimate.
Weakness in China and declining momentum across the Jordan brand weighed on results, while management warned of a high-single-digit revenue decline for the current fiscal year.
The revenue miss overshadowed an earnings beat, with shares extending their losses in after-hours trading.
Corteva suffered an especially sharp decline, losing more than 80% after completing the spin-off of its Vylor seed business, leaving the company as a standalone crop protection business.
In after-hours trading, Synaptics gained more than 14% following a revised merger agreement with onsemi, valuing the transaction at approximately $5.7 billion.

EUROPE: DAX FALLS TO LOWEST LEVEL SINCE JULY AS OIL AND BOND YIELDS WEIGH
European equities delivered a considerably weaker performance than their US counterparts.
Germany’s DAX 40 dropped approximately 1% on Thursday, closing at 24,939 and reaching its lowest level since July 23.
Selling pressure was driven primarily by higher energy prices, elevated bond yields and deteriorating geopolitical conditions in the Middle East.
Additional concerns came from accelerating inflation across several major European economies, potentially forcing the European Central Bank to maintain restrictive monetary conditions for longer than previously anticipated.
Almost every sector ended in negative territory, with pharmaceuticals and healthcare, banks and automotive stocks among the weakest performers.
Bayer fell 5.2%, Volkswagen declined 3.4%, Merck lost 2.6%, Deutsche Bank dropped 2.4%, while Fresenius SE & Co slipped approximately 2.3%.
Infineon Technologies also closed slightly lower. On the upside, Heidelberg Materials gained 3% after receiving a positive rating from JPMorgan.

OIL: WTI ABOVE $92 AS GEOPOLITICAL RISK RETURNS TO THE FOREFRONT
The energy sector remains one of the most important areas of focus for global markets.
WTI crude settled at $92.87 a barrel on Thursday, while Brent remained above $102, extending the gains recorded over the previous two sessions.
The main driver remains growing concern over a potential escalation in the conflict between the United States and Iran.
According to reports, Washington is considering deploying a second aircraft carrier and approximately 10,000 additional military personnel to the Middle East, providing the administration with further military options.
Reports suggesting that the United States could resume attacks against Iran after the November midterm elections have added another layer of uncertainty.
The main concern for the oil market remains the sustainability of the recovery in Middle Eastern energy flows. Although exports have shown signs of returning toward pre-conflict levels, market participants remain cautious, particularly in the absence of a lasting agreement.
At least three tankers were reportedly attacked this week while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran and its Houthi allies have continued targeting refining infrastructure across the region.
China’s decision to suspend fuel exports adds another potential source of pressure to the refined products market.
For crude oil, therefore, the issue is not simply the current level of inventories or production. The key question is whether renewed logistical disruptions and infrastructure damage could once again threaten physical supply.

GOLD: DOLLAR STRENGTH AND HIGHER YIELDS LIMIT RECOVERY
Gold traded around $4,150 an ounce on Friday, heading toward its second consecutive weekly decline.
The precious metal continues to face pressure from a stronger US dollar and elevated Treasury yields, both of which reduce the relative attractiveness of a non-yielding asset.
Interestingly, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East have so far failed to provide sufficient support to offset these headwinds.
Rising oil prices are instead fueling concerns about renewed inflationary pressure and the possibility that the Federal Reserve may need to keep interest rates elevated for longer.
Recent comments from Neel Kashkari, President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, have also kept attention focused on monetary policy. Kashkari emphasized that it remains unclear how high interest rates will need to rise to bring inflation back under control.
Investors will therefore need to assess the interaction between geopolitical risk, inflation and the cost of capital.

FOREX: US DOLLAR INDEX ABOVE 102, HEADING FOR THIRD CONSECUTIVE WEEKLY GAIN
The US Dollar Index strengthened above 102 on Friday, putting it on track for a third consecutive week of gains.
The greenback is benefiting from the relative resilience of the US economy, rising Treasury yields and increased demand for liquidity amid growing international uncertainty.
Interest-rate differentials continue to support the dollar against other major currencies, while investors await clearer signals about the direction of US monetary policy.
September’s employment report will therefore be an important catalyst for the currency market. Particularly strong data could reinforce expectations of higher-for-longer interest rates, while signs of labor market weakness could reopen the debate over future monetary easing.

TECHNOLOGY AND AI: ANTHROPIC REPORTEDLY CONSIDERS STOCK MARKET LISTING
In the technology sector, attention has also turned to Anthropic, which is reportedly exploring the possibility of going public as early as mid-November.
A potential IPO would represent another significant development for the artificial intelligence industry, at a time when investment in AI infrastructure, semiconductors and cloud services continues to drive a substantial portion of technology market activity.
The news comes as investors become increasingly selective, distinguishing between companies capable of converting AI-related demand into tangible revenue and earnings growth and those still relying heavily on future expectations.

MARKET OUTLOOK: US LABOR DATA, THE FED AND GEOPOLITICS TO SHAPE THE NEXT MARKET DIRECTION
The current market environment remains heavily influenced by three closely interconnected variables: the US labor market, Treasury yields and geopolitical risk.
September’s employment report could reshape expectations for the Federal Reserve, although its impact will also depend on wage growth and the broader employment trend.
At the same time, crude oil holding sustainably above the $90–$100 range could keep inflation expectations elevated, potentially limiting the Federal Reserve’s room for maneuver.
For Wall Street, resilient corporate earnings and economic growth remain important sources of support. However, rising Treasury yields represent an increasing risk to equity valuations, particularly if they coincide with a slowdown in economic activity.
Internationally, the Middle East remains a major source of uncertainty. Any further escalation could quickly increase the geopolitical risk premium in oil prices, creating knock-on effects across inflation, bonds, currencies and equity markets.

In summary, markets are facing an increasingly delicate balance: resilient economic growth, Treasury yields at their highest levels in more than two decades and an energy-related geopolitical risk that continues to represent a potential source of instability.
